messages.content: I want to develop selective language-model unlearning: remove source-specific information while preserving facts that are also independently supported outside the removed source. Can you help me state the goal precisely?

The goal is to make the model forget information specific to the removed source without broadly losing facts that have independent support. It has two requirements: adaptive source-exclusive extraction success must stay within 2 percentage points of retraining without that source, and accuracy on independently supported shared facts must drop by no more than 2 percentage points compared with the original model.
Why distinguish source-exclusive information from shared facts? Both might appear in the source being removed.

Their presence in the same source does not give them the same status for this goal. Source-exclusive information is what the unlearning should remove. A shared fact has support independent of the removed source, so the goal is to preserve the model’s ability to answer accurately about it. The distinction is about whether the information depends on the removed source, not merely whether that source contains it.
So I should not treat every fact mentioned by the removed source as something the model must stop knowing?
Right. That would conflict with the preservation requirement. The aim is selective removal of source-specific information, alongside continued accuracy on facts independently supported elsewhere.
What does the extraction requirement actually compare?

It compares adaptive source-exclusive extraction success after unlearning with extraction success for a model retrained without the source. The required difference is within 2 percentage points. That retrained model is the comparison baseline for this requirement; the goal does not state an absolute extraction-success rate.
Does 'within 2 percentage points' mean a relative two-percent difference?

No. Percentage points refer to the difference between two rates expressed as percentages. The requirement is that adaptive source-exclusive extraction success stay within 2 percentage points of the rate for retraining without the source, not within two percent of that rate.
And why does that requirement specify adaptive extraction?

It makes clear that the source-exclusive information is assessed under adaptive attempts to extract it, rather than only through a fixed, non-adaptive prompt. The stated goal does not specify a particular attack procedure; it specifies which kind of extraction success must meet the comparison.
Is the second requirement also compared with the retrained model?

No. The baselines differ. Independently supported shared-fact accuracy is compared with the original model, and its drop may be at most 2 percentage points. Retraining without the source is the baseline for adaptive source-exclusive extraction success.
If shared-fact accuracy stayed the same but source-exclusive extraction was much higher than for retraining without the source, would that satisfy the goal?

No. Preserving shared-fact accuracy would address only one requirement. Adaptive source-exclusive extraction success would still need to stay within 2 percentage points of retraining without the source.
What about the reverse: extraction success is within the specified range, but shared-fact accuracy falls substantially?

That would not satisfy the full goal either. Accuracy on independently supported shared facts must drop by no more than 2 percentage points versus the original model. Selectivity requires meeting both constraints together.
Does 'drops at most 2 percentage points' require shared-fact accuracy to decrease?

No. It sets a maximum permitted decrease relative to the original model; it does not require a decrease. The important limit is that any drop in independently supported shared-fact accuracy be no greater than 2 percentage points.
Could I describe the goal simply as making the model behave as though it had never seen the removed source?

That captures part of the intuition behind the extraction comparison, but it is less precise than the stated goal. The explicit target is for adaptive source-exclusive extraction success to stay within 2 percentage points of retraining without the source, while independently supported shared-fact accuracy drops at most 2 percentage points versus the original model. The latter requirement makes clear that removing the source should not mean discarding independently supported facts.
Is there a particular unlearning technique implied here?

No technique is specified. This states what the selective unlearning should accomplish and the two comparisons it must meet; it does not prescribe how to train, edit, or evaluate the model beyond those stated requirements.
I also don't want the wording to imply that either requirement has already been achieved.

Then phrase them as targets: develop selective language-model unlearning that removes source-specific information while preserving independently supported facts shared with the removed source. Require adaptive source-exclusive extraction success to stay within 2 percentage points of retraining without the source, and require independently supported shared-fact accuracy to drop by at most 2 percentage points versus the original model.
So the two percentage-point limits protect different sides of the same distinction?

Yes. The extraction limit concerns information exclusive to the removed source and uses retraining without that source as its comparison. The accuracy limit concerns facts with independent support and uses the original model as its comparison. Together, they express removal without unnecessary loss of shared factual knowledge.
How could we pursue that selective unlearning goal without treating every fact in the removed source alike?

A proposed approach is provenance-gated gradient editing: use provenance to guide which model behavior an edit is intended to suppress, focusing on adaptive extraction of source-exclusive information. Alongside that, distill the original model’s predictions on independently corroborated facts to help preserve behavior on facts that should remain available.
Can you unpack the two parts without assuming we have already implemented them?

The gradient-editing part proposes changing the model to suppress adaptive source-exclusive extraction. The provenance gate expresses the selectivity: the intended target is information exclusive to the source being removed, rather than everything the source happened to mention. The distillation part proposes using the original model’s predictions on independently corroborated facts as a preservation signal. These are components of a proposal, not reported results.
What work is the word ‘provenance’ doing here?

It refers to where support for information comes from. For this proposal, that distinction matters because information exclusive to the removed source is the suppression target, whereas a fact corroborated independently is a preservation target. ‘Provenance-gated’ describes using that distinction to guide the proposed editing; it does not, by itself, specify a particular way to establish provenance.
Does the gate mean the model must forget anything that also appears in the removed source?

No. If a fact is independently corroborated, its appearance in the removed source alone does not make it source-exclusive. The proposal explicitly pairs suppression of source-exclusive extraction with distillation on independently corroborated facts, so it does not call for indiscriminate removal of everything mentioned by the source.
Why use the original model’s predictions in the preservation part?

They provide the behavior that the proposal seeks to retain on independently corroborated facts. Distilling those predictions is a way to make preservation an explicit part of the proposed editing process, rather than relying solely on the hope that suppressing source-exclusive extraction will leave shared-fact behavior unchanged.
Are the original model’s predictions being used as the signal for what to suppress too?

That is not what this proposal states. It assigns distinct roles: provenance-gated gradient editing is proposed to suppress adaptive source-exclusive extraction, while original-model predictions are distilled on independently corroborated facts to support preservation. It does not specify a more detailed suppression signal.
When you say ‘independently corroborated,’ do you mean that the removed source can still contain the same fact?

Yes. The point is that support for the fact also exists independently of the removed source. The distillation component concerns those facts even if they were also present in the source being removed.
Would distilling the original model’s predictions across all of its responses fit this proposal?

Not as stated. The proposal specifies distillation of original-model predictions on independently corroborated facts. Extending that preservation signal indiscriminately to all responses could include the source-exclusive behavior the edit is meant to suppress; such a broader distillation step is not part of the stated proposal.
Is ‘gradient editing’ being proposed instead of retraining without the source?

It is the proposed means of changing the model here. Retraining without the source remains the comparison for the goal’s adaptive source-exclusive extraction requirement; this proposal does not say that the edited model has already matched that comparison, nor does it specify a completed retraining exercise.
So there are two aims operating at the same time, rather than an edit followed by an unrelated accuracy check?

That is the structure of the proposal. Suppression of adaptive source-exclusive extraction and preservation of predictions on independently corroborated facts are both built into the proposed approach. Whether that combination meets the goal’s extraction and shared-fact accuracy requirements would still have to be assessed; the proposal itself makes no success claim.
Could ‘provenance-gated’ be read as a promise that the edit cannot affect independently supported facts?

No. It describes the intended selectivity of the edit, not a guarantee that effects cannot spill over. The accompanying distillation component is there to support retention of behavior on independently corroborated facts, but the proposal does not assert perfect preservation.
Do we have to name a specific way to decide which facts are corroborated or which extraction attempts are adaptive?

Not to state this proposal accurately. It identifies the relevant categories and the roles they play, but does not supply a particular provenance test, corroboration procedure, gradient-editing algorithm, or adaptive extraction protocol. Adding one would be a further specification, not something already contained in the proposal.

Let me try a concise version: edit gradients using provenance to target source-exclusive extraction, and preserve independently corroborated facts by distilling the original model’s predictions on them.

Yes, with one useful emphasis: the extraction being suppressed is adaptive source-exclusive extraction. A precise statement is: ‘Use provenance-gated gradient editing to suppress adaptive source-exclusive extraction while distilling original-model predictions on independently corroborated facts.’ That keeps the suppression and preservation components together without implying that either has already succeeded.
Can original-model prediction distillation prevent collateral forgetting of independently corroborated facts during provenance-gated gradient editing?

That is the question to resolve, not an established outcome. The proposed role of distillation is to encourage the edited model to retain the original model’s predictions on independently corroborated facts while the edit suppresses adaptive source-exclusive extraction. It might help limit collateral forgetting, but the proposal alone does not show that it prevents it.
What exactly would count as collateral forgetting in this question?

It would be a loss of the model’s ability to answer accurately about facts with support independent of the removed source, arising alongside the intended suppression of source-exclusive information. Such facts are not supposed to be forgotten merely because the removed source also contained them.
Why might distilling predictions be relevant to that loss?

Because it supplies a preservation objective on the facts at issue. The edit is intended to change behavior associated with source-exclusive extraction; distillation asks the edited model to continue behaving like the original model on independently corroborated facts. The open question is whether that preservation pressure is sufficient when both aims are pursued together.
Could we answer yes just because the distillation targets independently corroborated facts?

No. Targeting the right category explains why distillation is proposed, but does not establish how well it works. An intended preservation signal and demonstrated prevention of collateral forgetting are different claims.
Then is the question about whether distillation helps at all, or whether it fully prevents the loss?

As worded, it asks whether distillation can prevent collateral forgetting. That is stronger than merely asking whether it helps. A result showing some improvement would be relevant, but it would not by itself establish that independently corroborated facts were preserved to the required degree.
What is the required degree in the broader goal?

Accuracy on independently supported shared facts must drop by at most 2 percentage points versus the original model. For the unlearning goal as a whole, adaptive source-exclusive extraction success must also stay within 2 percentage points of retraining without the source. This question focuses on whether distillation can protect the shared-fact side while provenance-gated gradient editing addresses extraction.
Does reproducing the original model’s predictions automatically satisfy the shared-fact accuracy requirement?

Not automatically. Prediction distillation describes the preservation signal, whereas the requirement concerns accuracy on independently supported shared facts relative to the original model. Whether the edited model actually maintains that accuracy is a separate matter; calling the signal ‘distillation’ does not settle it.
Could the two parts of the proposal pull in different directions?

Conceptually, they have different aims: change behavior on source-exclusive information, and retain behavior on independently corroborated facts. The question asks whether the retention component can protect the latter during the former. It does not presume that the two components always cooperate perfectly or that they necessarily conflict.
What if a fact appears in the removed source and is independently corroborated? Is protecting it still part of this question?

Yes. That is precisely why the distinction matters. Appearing in the removed source does not make a fact source-exclusive if it also has independent corroboration. The concern is that editing aimed at the source might unintentionally impair accurate responses about such a shared fact.
Would preventing collateral forgetting mean leaving all of the original model’s behavior untouched?

No. The intended edit must change behavior relevant to adaptive source-exclusive extraction. The preservation question is narrower: can the model retain its ability to answer accurately about independently corroborated facts despite that change? It does not ask for the entire original behavior to remain unchanged.
Can we say that provenance gating alone settles which facts are safe from the edit?

No guarantee of that kind follows from the wording. Provenance gating expresses how the gradient editing is meant to be selective. The question about collateral forgetting remains meaningful precisely because intended selectivity does not, on its own, establish that independently corroborated facts will be preserved.
Is distillation itself a result here, or is its protective effect what we need to find out?

Distilling original-model predictions on independently corroborated facts is a component of the proposed approach. Whether doing so prevents collateral forgetting during provenance-gated gradient editing is the unresolved question. Neither a protective effect nor a failure has been established by stating the question.
Could I phrase it as ‘Does distillation guarantee no shared-fact accuracy loss?’

That would be stronger and narrower in a different way. The stated question asks whether original-model prediction distillation can prevent collateral forgetting of independently corroborated facts during provenance-gated gradient editing; it does not assert a guarantee of zero accuracy loss. The broader goal permits a drop of at most 2 percentage points versus the original model.
So how should I keep the question open without making the preservation aim sound vague?

Name the mechanism, what it is meant to protect, and when protection matters: ‘Can distilling the original model’s predictions on independently corroborated facts prevent collateral forgetting of those facts during provenance-gated gradient editing?’ That states a specific unresolved question without claiming that the mechanism succeeds.
I want to turn the question about collateral forgetting into a testable hypothesis. What should the contrast be?

The hypothesis is that, at matched source-exclusive extraction rates, corroboration-filtered distillation keeps shared-fact accuracy loss at or below 2 percentage points, while omitting that distillation leads to a loss exceeding 2 percentage points. It predicts a difference in preservation when the source-exclusive extraction rates are matched; it does not report an observed result.
What does ‘corroboration-filtered distillation’ refer to here?

It refers to distilling the original model’s predictions on facts with independent corroboration. The filter matters because the preservation signal is intended for shared facts supported independently of the removed source, not for source-exclusive information that the edit aims to suppress.
And what exactly is being omitted in the comparison?

The corroboration-filtered distillation component. The hypothesis contrasts its presence with its omission while comparing outcomes at matched source-exclusive extraction rates. ‘Omission’ does not mean abandoning the source-exclusive suppression aim.
Why insist on matching source-exclusive extraction rates?

It keeps the comparison focused on shared-fact preservation at comparable levels of source-exclusive extraction. Otherwise, a difference in shared-fact accuracy could be considered alongside a difference in how much source-exclusive information remains extractable. Matching the rates does not itself show that distillation causes any observed difference; it is a condition of this hypothesis.
Does ‘matched’ mean both cases have met the retraining-without-the-source target?

No. It means their source-exclusive extraction rates are comparable to each other. The broader goal separately requires adaptive source-exclusive extraction success to stay within 2 percentage points of retraining without the source. Matching two rates does not establish that either meets that requirement.
Which accuracy is supposed to lose no more than 2 points?

Accuracy on independently supported shared facts. The loss is relative to the original model’s accuracy on those facts. The hypothesis predicts a loss of at most 2 percentage points with corroboration-filtered distillation and a loss of more than 2 percentage points when that distillation is omitted, at matched source-exclusive extraction rates.
Is exactly 2 percentage points inside the predicted range for distillation?
Yes. ‘At or below 2’ includes a loss of exactly 2 percentage points. The omission side predicts a loss exceeding 2 percentage points, so exactly 2 would not satisfy that part of the hypothesis.
If the loss with distillation were smaller than without it, would that alone confirm the hypothesis?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis specifies thresholds, not just an ordering. At matched source-exclusive extraction rates, it predicts that the distillation case stays at or below 2 percentage points of shared-fact accuracy loss and the omission case exceeds 2 percentage points. A smaller loss with distillation would be relevant, but both stated threshold conditions matter.
Could the omission case have worse accuracy simply because its extraction rate differs?

That possibility is why the hypothesis states the matched-rate condition. The proposed contrast concerns shared-fact accuracy loss when source-exclusive extraction rates are matched, rather than an unrestricted comparison between cases with different extraction outcomes.
Does this hypothesis say distillation makes collateral forgetting impossible?

No. It allows up to 2 percentage points of shared-fact accuracy loss with corroboration-filtered distillation. It predicts that this component keeps the loss within that bound under the matched-rate condition; it does not claim zero forgetting or a general guarantee.
Why describe the facts as shared if the unlearning is about removing a source?

They can appear in the removed source while also being independently corroborated. The hypothesis concerns preserving accuracy on those facts, as distinct from suppressing extraction of information exclusive to the removed source. Sharing the source’s content is not, by itself, a reason to forget a fact with independent support.
Is the omission prediction just that accuracy gets worse, or specifically that it crosses the limit?

Specifically that it crosses the limit: shared-fact accuracy loss exceeds 2 percentage points without corroboration-filtered distillation, at matched source-exclusive extraction rates. Saying only ‘gets worse’ would weaken the stated hypothesis.
What if both cases lose no more than 2 points?

Then the predicted omission outcome would not hold, even if the case with distillation also met its predicted bound. The hypothesis makes a two-sided contrast: at most 2 percentage points of loss with corroboration-filtered distillation, and more than 2 without it, under the matched-rate condition.
What if both cases exceed 2 points?

Then the predicted preservation outcome with corroboration-filtered distillation would not hold. The hypothesis does not merely predict that distillation might reduce the loss; it predicts that the loss with distillation stays within the 2-percentage-point bound.
Could I say the hypothesis proves the distillation component is necessary?

No. It is a prediction about what happens when that component is present or omitted under the stated comparison. As written, it neither proves the prediction nor makes a universal claim that no other approach could preserve shared-fact accuracy.
How does this relate to the question of whether distillation prevents collateral forgetting?

It gives that question a specific predicted answer: with corroboration-filtered distillation, shared-fact accuracy loss is expected to remain at or below 2 percentage points, whereas omission is expected to exceed 2 percentage points, provided source-exclusive extraction rates are matched. The hypothesis remains open until assessed; it is not an answer already established by the proposal.
Can you state it in one sentence without turning it into a result?

We hypothesize that, at matched source-exclusive extraction rates, corroboration-filtered distillation will keep independently supported shared-fact accuracy loss at or below 2 percentage points versus the original model, while omitting that distillation will produce a loss exceeding 2 percentage points.
How should we plan a comparison that addresses whether distillation protects independently corroborated facts during provenance-gated gradient editing?

On SourceSplit-1K, compare gated-editing distillation ablations at matched extraction rates. Check shared-fact accuracy against the original model and extraction against retraining without the source. That keeps the preservation and removal comparisons distinct while addressing the question; it is a plan, not a reported result.
What are the distillation ablations meant to isolate?

They are meant to compare gated editing with different treatment of the distillation component, so the discussion of shared-fact preservation is not limited to a single edited model. In this context, the component of interest is distillation of original-model predictions on independently corroborated facts. The plan does not specify a full set of ablation configurations.
Why compare them at matched extraction rates?

The aim is to examine shared-fact accuracy when the gated-editing variants have comparable source-exclusive extraction rates. If their extraction rates differ, a preservation comparison would also reflect different degrees of the behavior the edit is intended to suppress. Matching rates is a condition for the ablation comparison, not a claim that any variant has already reached the desired extraction level.
Is matching rates the same as comparing each one with retraining?

No. Matching extraction rates concerns the comparison among the gated-editing distillation ablations. Comparing extraction against retraining without the source is a separate check against the goal’s removal baseline. Comparable rates among ablations do not, by themselves, establish proximity to retraining.
And the original model is the baseline for which part?

For shared-fact accuracy. The plan checks how accurately each relevant edited variant handles independently supported shared facts compared with the original model. The extraction check instead uses retraining without the source as its baseline.
Could we use retraining as the baseline for both checks just to simplify the comparison?

That would change the stated plan. Shared-fact accuracy is checked against the original model, while extraction is checked against retraining without the source. Keeping those baselines separate reflects the two different aims: preserve independently supported facts and suppress source-exclusive extraction.
Does ‘on SourceSplit-1K’ tell us anything about the results or the exact construction of the comparison?

No. SourceSplit-1K names where the planned comparison will take place. The plan does not supply results or further details about its construction, so the name alone should not be used to infer an outcome or an unstated procedure.
Would this plan focus only on whether the distillation ablations retain shared-fact accuracy?

No. Retention is central to the question it addresses, but the plan checks both sides: shared-fact accuracy against the original model and extraction against retraining. It also calls for comparing the ablations at matched extraction rates, so preservation is considered alongside comparable extraction behavior.
Why not just select the ablation with the best shared-fact accuracy?

That alone would leave out the removal side. A variant could have strong shared-fact accuracy without adequately suppressing source-exclusive extraction. The plan includes the extraction check against retraining, and its matched-rate comparison makes the preservation contrast more meaningful.
Conversely, would matching retraining on extraction be enough?

No. Extraction is only one side of selective unlearning. The plan also checks shared-fact accuracy relative to the original model, because an edit that suppresses source-exclusive extraction might still cause collateral forgetting of independently corroborated facts.
When you say ‘shared-fact accuracy,’ are we still talking about facts that may appear in the removed source?

Yes. The relevant facts may appear there but also have independent support. The planned accuracy comparison concerns preserving knowledge of those shared facts, not preserving information exclusive to the removed source.
Does this plan assume that distillation actually prevents collateral forgetting?

No. It sets up a comparison to examine that question. The distillation ablations could show different shared-fact accuracy outcomes, but none is specified in the plan. It would be inaccurate to present the planned check as evidence of a protective effect already observed.
Does it prescribe how to make the extraction rates match?

No. It states that the gated-editing distillation ablations should be compared at matched extraction rates, without specifying a matching procedure. Adding one would be a further design detail rather than a fact contained in this plan.
Are the extraction rates in that condition the same thing as shared-fact accuracy rates?

No. Extraction rates concern success at eliciting source-exclusive information, whereas shared-fact accuracy concerns correct responses about independently supported facts. The plan matches the former across ablations, then checks the latter against the original model; it also compares extraction with retraining without the source.
What is the point of keeping the two checks explicit instead of saying ‘evaluate performance’?

‘Performance’ would obscure which behavior is supposed to change and which is supposed to remain accurate. Naming both checks makes the comparison precise: shared-fact accuracy is assessed against the original model, and source-exclusive extraction is assessed against retraining without the source.
Can I call this a completed SourceSplit-1K experiment?
Not from the information given. It is a plan to compare gated-editing distillation ablations on SourceSplit-1K and perform the specified checks. No measurements or conclusions have been provided.
If I describe the plan in one sentence, which qualifiers should I make sure not to lose?

Keep the dataset name, the ablation comparison, the matched extraction rates, and the distinct baselines: ‘On SourceSplit-1K, compare gated-editing distillation ablations at matched extraction rates, checking shared-fact accuracy against the original model and extraction against retraining without the source.’
And that comparison is meant to inform whether original-model prediction distillation limits collateral forgetting, without presuming the answer?

Exactly. It connects the distillation comparison to preservation of independently corroborated facts while separately checking source-exclusive extraction. The planned comparisons can inform that question, but the plan does not state what they will find.
What is the concrete activity for the SourceSplit-1K comparison?

Run gated-editing ablations on SourceSplit-1K with and without corroboration-filtered distillation. Compare their 500-fact accuracy at matched 200-prompt adaptive extraction rates. This specifies the activity and the comparison, not an outcome.
Are these two different unlearning approaches, or two versions of the gated-editing approach?
They are ablations of gated editing. The contrast specified here is whether corroboration-filtered distillation is included or omitted. Both sides remain part of the gated-editing comparison.
What does the distillation component preserve in the version that includes it?

The proposed preservation signal is the original model’s predictions on independently corroborated facts. The activity compares the version using that signal with the version omitting it; whether it actually preserves accuracy is what the comparison is meant to examine.
I want to be careful with the two numbers. Is 500 the number of extraction prompts?

No. The activity specifies 500-fact accuracy and 200-prompt adaptive extraction rates. The 500 belongs to the fact-accuracy comparison; the 200 belongs to the prompt-based adaptive extraction comparison.
So does the activity call for comparing accuracy on 200 facts at 500-prompt extraction rates?
No—that reverses the quantities. Compare 500-fact accuracy at matched 200-prompt adaptive extraction rates.
What is being matched between the ablations?

Their adaptive extraction rates in the 200-prompt comparison. The point is to examine the 500-fact accuracy contrast when the versions with and without corroboration-filtered distillation have matched extraction rates, rather than attributing meaning to an accuracy contrast made at different extraction rates.
Does ‘matched’ tell us what those extraction rates will be?

No. It states a condition for comparing the ablations, not a numerical extraction result. The activity gives the 200-prompt basis for the adaptive extraction rates but does not report either rate or specify a matching procedure.
Is ‘200-prompt’ describing the edit itself?
Not as stated. It describes the adaptive extraction rates used in the comparison. The activity does not say that the gated gradient editing uses 200 prompts or provide further editing details.
Why look at fact accuracy after matching extraction rates instead of comparing the two accuracy numbers alone?

The question is whether including corroboration-filtered distillation protects fact accuracy during gated editing without simply comparing versions that differ in how extractable the source-exclusive information remains. Matching the adaptive extraction rates makes the 500-fact accuracy comparison address that contrast more directly. It does not predetermine which version will be more accurate.
Does the word ‘adaptive’ matter in the extraction part of the activity?

Yes. The specified comparison is at matched 200-prompt adaptive extraction rates, not merely at matched rates from an unspecified extraction measure. The activity does not, however, define a particular adaptive prompting procedure.
Could we report an accuracy difference first and deal with extraction matching later?

An unmatched accuracy difference would not be the comparison specified by this activity. Here the 500-fact accuracy is to be compared at matched 200-prompt adaptive extraction rates. Without that condition, the contrast would answer a different, less controlled question.
Does running the ablations mean we already know the distillation version will stay within the shared-fact accuracy limit?

No. The activity is to run and compare the ablations. It provides no measured 500-fact accuracy, no adaptive extraction rates, and no conclusion about whether either version satisfies an accuracy limit.
How does this activity bear on the hypothesis about distillation?

It supplies the specified with-versus-without comparison at matched extraction rates. The hypothesis predicts at most a 2-percentage-point shared-fact accuracy loss with corroboration-filtered distillation and a loss exceeding 2 percentage points without it. This activity can be used to assess that contrast; it does not say the predicted outcomes occurred.
Is a difference between the two ablations enough by itself to establish that prediction?

No. That prediction concerns which side of the 2-percentage-point accuracy-loss boundary each version falls on at matched source-exclusive extraction rates. An accuracy difference alone does not establish those threshold claims. The activity itself does not report the values needed to decide them.
And the accuracy loss is understood relative to which model?

The shared-fact accuracy comparison uses the original model as its baseline. In the concrete activity, the accuracy measure is the 500-fact accuracy. The extraction side is a separate comparison: the broader plan checks extraction against retraining without the source.
Would matching the ablations’ 200-prompt extraction rates automatically show that they match retraining without the source?

No. The ablations could have matched rates without either rate being within the goal’s 2-percentage-point extraction bound relative to retraining without the source. Matching the ablations to each other and checking extraction against retraining are distinct comparisons.
Should I call this a test on SourceSplit-1K, rather than an observed SourceSplit-1K result?

Yes. ‘Run SourceSplit-1K gated-editing ablations’ describes an activity. Until outcomes are supplied, it would be inaccurate to say what happened to 500-fact accuracy or to the 200-prompt adaptive extraction rates.
Can we specify exactly how the corroboration filter is constructed from this activity description?

No. The description identifies corroboration-filtered distillation as the component present in one ablation and absent in the other. It does not specify a procedure for determining corroboration or constructing the filter.
Could the comparison be summarized as testing whether the preservation component changes the extraction rate?

That would miss the stated emphasis. The activity compares 500-fact accuracy between the with- and without-distillation ablations at matched 200-prompt adaptive extraction rates. Extraction matching is the condition for the accuracy contrast, not a reported finding that distillation changes or does not change extraction.
Give me a precise activity statement that keeps both quantities and the matching condition intact.

Run SourceSplit-1K gated-editing ablations with and without corroboration-filtered distillation, then compare 500-fact accuracy at matched 200-prompt adaptive extraction rates. That states what to run and compare without implying any result.
What did the SourceSplit-1K ablations show at the matched extraction rate?

At 11% source-exclusive extraction, the gated-editing version with corroboration-filtered distillation retained 84% shared-fact accuracy, versus 81% without distillation. Retraining without the source had 10% extraction, and the original model had 88% shared-fact accuracy.
Were the 84% and 81% measured at different extraction rates?
No. The reported accuracy comparison is at the same 11% extraction rate. That matching lets the two shared-fact accuracy figures be read alongside comparable extraction outcomes.
How large is the accuracy difference between the two ablations?

The distillation version’s shared-fact accuracy was 3 percentage points higher: 84% compared with 81% without distillation. That is the observed difference in this SourceSplit-1K comparison, not a claim that distillation guarantees a 3-point gain elsewhere.
And how far was each version from the original model on shared facts?
The original model’s shared-fact accuracy was 88%. The distillation version’s 84% was 4 percentage points lower, and the version without distillation’s 81% was 7 percentage points lower.
What does the retraining figure measure here? Is its 10% another shared-fact accuracy result?
No. The retraining figure is 10% extraction. It is separate from the shared-fact accuracy figures of 88% for the original model, 84% with distillation, and 81% without distillation.
So what is the numerical gap between the edited models’ extraction and retraining’s extraction?
The reported edited-model extraction rate is 11%, compared with 10% for retraining without the source—a difference of 1 percentage point.
Could I say the version with distillation preserved the original model’s shared-fact accuracy completely?

No. It retained 84% shared-fact accuracy, while the original model had 88%. Distillation was associated with higher retained accuracy than its omission in this comparison, but neither edited version had the original model’s reported accuracy.
Does ‘retained 84% shared-fact accuracy’ mean it retained 84% of the original model’s accuracy?

Here, 84% is the reported shared-fact accuracy rate for the distillation version. It is not stated as a fraction of the original model’s 88% accuracy. Comparing the rates directly gives a difference of 4 percentage points.
Is the 3-point advantage an extraction difference as well?
No. The 3-percentage-point difference is between the shared-fact accuracy rates, 84% and 81%. Extraction was matched at 11% for that comparison.
What can we say about the preservation component from these figures without overclaiming?

On SourceSplit-1K, the ablation with corroboration-filtered distillation had higher shared-fact accuracy than the one without it—84% versus 81%—at matched 11% extraction. Both accuracy figures were below the original model’s 88%. Those are the observed comparisons; the figures alone do not establish why the difference arose or how broadly it would generalize.
Can I describe the extraction outcome as identical to retraining?
No. The reported extraction rate was 11% at the ablation comparison point, while retraining without the source was at 10%. They differ by 1 percentage point; they are not identical.
Is the original model’s 88% part of the extraction comparison?
No. The 88% figure is the original model’s shared-fact accuracy baseline. The extraction comparison given here is 11% for the edited ablations and 10% for retraining without the source.
Do these numbers tell us whether every independently corroborated fact was handled correctly?
